The Stokes–Einstein (or Stokes–Einstein–Sutherland, SES) relation connects the self-diffusion coefficient D of particles in a liquid to the liquid's shear viscosity η through d = k<sub>B</sub> T/(2πηD), where d is an effective hydrodynamic diameter. It follows from combining the Einstein relation for Brownian motion with Stokes drag on a sphere, so it assumes independent, randomly moving, roughly spherical particles. In many liquids d is nearly constant over a temperature range, which lets one property be estimated from the other. A common generalization is the fractional Stokes–Einstein form D/T ∝ η<sup>(-κ)</sup>, where κ = 1 recovers the SES and smaller exponents (often 0.6 to 1) signal a breakdown. Deviations typically appear in supercooled or near-melting liquids, and their origin (local structure, dynamic heterogeneity, species decoupling) is debated. Computing D and η from simulation is covered under [transport properties from molecular dynamics](/papers/topics/molecular-dynamics-transport-properties/), and one structural explanation is [icosahedral order](/papers/topics/icosahedral-order-in-liquids/).

## Deviation in liquid Al–Si from icosahedral clusters (2022)

Zhan and Kitchin used classical molecular dynamics of Al0.90Si0.10 and Al0.94Si0.06 to show that the effective diameter is constant from about 1400 K to the melting point (630 K and 700 K in their model) and deviates below it, with a fitted κ of 0.97 ± 0.01. Per-atom transport estimates showed that icosahedral clusters raise the viscosity but leave diffusion unchanged, and excluding cluster atoms restored κ to 1.00 ± 0.02 and 0.99 ± 0.02, identifying the clusters as the origin of the deviation ([Zhan 2021](/papers/zhan2022b/)). Summary: [zhan2022b](/papers/zhan2022b/).
